title: Never Start an Email With “Hope You’re Well” | Stanford Writing Professor
guest: Glenn Kramon, Stanford GSB lecturer ('Winning Writing') and former New York Times editor of 37 years
summary: Stanford GSB writing lecturer Glenn Kramon gives a masterclass on business email: why 'hope you are well' makes you one of a million, his 12 rules for email, golden rules for cold emails (lead with how you can help, drop names, use 'like you'), how to follow up without giving up, and why gratitude letters to people who helped you long ago are his favorite assignment. Main takeaway: in the age of AI everyone's default writing has improved, so you must be 'one in a million' through warmth, competence and handmade personalization.

ideas.idea: Never open an email with 'hope you are well'; the first five words must make the reader smile or get to the point, and pleasantries belong at the end.
ideas.detail: At least half of his Stanford class admits to the habit, and AI does it too, so it makes you 'one of a million'. People read on phones and may only see five words; 'cheers' or 'hope you're well' at the sign-off means the same thing without wasting the opening. The colder the email, the more important it is to get straight into it.

ideas.idea: Open cold emails with a researched, non-offensive personal connection that makes the recipient ask 'how did she know that?'
ideas.detail: He opened with Cherie by asking if she worked with Evan Spiegel. Use LinkedIn, Instagram and, best of all, people who know the target; a student had been babysat by the current Green Bay Packers coach. If the ask is too important to open with a hobby, put it in a PS so they leave feeling good, per Maya Angelou's line that people never forget how you made them feel.

ideas.idea: In the age of AI everybody's default writing has improved, so you must be even better than that baseline to stand out as a communicator.
ideas.detail: Kramon encourages students to use AI, but former students now managing teams call him complaining about 'AI slop' because everyone's emails sound the same; the hosts add that AI trains on existing writing and drags everyone to the same baseline.

ideas.idea: Do not let AI scare you off correct writing like the em dash or words like 'delve'; what your writing needs is your own voice.
ideas.detail: Students switched to hyphens to avoid looking AI-generated, but a hyphen is wrong and an em dash is correct. Cherie, who ran Dartmouth's peer writing program, says she edits out AI tics like 'so here's the ask:' but keeps the em dash.

ideas.idea: A one-in-a-million email combines warmth and competence, and competence is shown with specific cinematic examples, not vague labels.
ideas.detail: Instead of 'I'm resilient': 'my first startup went bankrupt and as a result I conserved cash and managed the most efficient early-stage sales team in biotech.' Instead of 'Swiss Army knife': 'at 17 I managed social media, customer retention, finance and HR for my family's diner struggling through COVID.' Examples via colleague Rachel Konrad.

ideas.idea: Instead of spraying 50 emails, pick the three to five people you most want a reply from and craft an undeniable email for each.
ideas.detail: A Slack salesperson ignored three times found the target loved telenovelas and paid the star Rogelio on Cameo to send a video message, and got her answer. Comedian Nardwuar gets rappers to open up by handing Snoop Dogg a VHS of his first movie and Pharrell his first album, 'Rump Shaker'.

ideas.idea: Kramon's 12 rules for email: know your audience; say what you like and would like; know your main point; clear personal urgent subject line; start with what they don't know; be more formal if unsure; start fast; be shorter; vary sentence length; write as you would speak to friends; add warmth or humor; assume it lands on page one of the New York Times.
ideas.detail: Jean read the full list from his Winning Writing lecture; rule 12 means write nothing you would not want distributed to everyone you know.

ideas.idea: Say what you like and what you would like, never what you don't like, because employees who hear 'I hate this' go defensive and stop listening.
ideas.detail: Start with praise, then the request; people who don't know your blunt style will route around you. In a performance review the sandwich bread is thick for strong performers, while for a troubled employee the middle dominates with concrete expectations and two-week and one-month check-ins.

ideas.idea: Subject lines must be personal and signal what matters to the recipient, because some people get 1,000 emails a day.
ideas.detail: Mention his favorite player Bryce Love and he will open it; 'my insights from our latest meeting' beats 'insights from latest meeting'. Fake-urgency subject lines like 'your account has been hacked' used to sell something are morally wrong and a bad practice.

ideas.idea: Start with what your audience doesn't know, not what it does, and get the ask into the first sentence.
ideas.detail: A pitch to Jeff Bezos opened with two paragraphs telling him he had transformed industries; the rewrite was 'Dear Mr. Bezos, I can help Alexa help patients needing personalized follow-up care. A Stanford MD/MBA, I'd appreciate a few minutes...'. Kramon met Bezos 25 years ago and notes Amazon's writing culture rejects time-wasting memos.

ideas.idea: The most common cold-email mistake is asking for something; instead show how you can help them, because it's about them, not you.
ideas.detail: Openers like 'I can expand your presence in Southeast Asia' or 'I've crunched the numbers and found a big business opportunity for you' keep people reading. Tim O'Brien, his first NYT hire (now running Bloomberg Opinion), walked into his interview with the first 10 stories he would write. Substitute 'company' for 'country' in JFK's 'ask not' line.

ideas.idea: Warm up a cold email by dropping names of mutual contacts, or better, getting that person to forward your email with an endorsement.
ideas.detail: People respond because they don't want to let down or anger their friend; the hosts cite 'our mutual friend Matt Abrahams suggested I speak with you' as their favorite tactic.

ideas.idea: The two most important words in a cold letter are 'like you', but the comparison must be specific, not generic.
ideas.detail: 'Like you, I started my entrepreneurial journey young: I bought candy wholesale and retailed it at school' or 'like you, I'm building a business in an industry where people like us are underrepresented' creates a visceral bond; 'like you, I believe AI will change our futures' is one of a million.

ideas.idea: A properly crafted email is handmade: it could only be received by that one person, even if the core body is reused across 20 recipients.
ideas.detail: Kramon called Jean's summary the most important point of the episode. Student Khalil Fuller's Gift Card Bank got supermarket CEOs to respond by noting one had started at the very bottom and likely knew Depression survivors; the nonprofit has since raised $80-100 million, including after the LA wildfires.

ideas.idea: When a cold email gets no reply, don't give up: follow up gently, add something fresh of value, and escalate subject lines to 'third try' or, for people you know, 'do I offend?'
ideas.detail: If no reply in the first few days, wait and send 'just ensuring you saw this' or a relevant new article. The few who never respond are people you probably don't want to work with anyway; Kramon himself has sent ten unanswered emails to Google co-founder Sergey Brin and now uses it as a class story.

ideas.idea: Always respond to email, even with 'thanks but no thanks', because non-responders are assumed to be arrogant, aloof or overwhelmed.
ideas.detail: Responders are assumed warm and personal and people want to work with them; anything beats ghosting. When he polls his class, more Stanford MBAs report being ghosted than ghosting.

ideas.idea: Write unexpected gratitude letters to people who helped you long ago, like a middle school teacher, because it moves them and empowers you.
ideas.detail: His NYT piece on gratitude notes got the biggest reaction of anything he's written; AI cannot write one because it doesn't hold your memories. Examples: a pregnant counselor who drove eight hours in rain to a college orientation, a commander who dragged her desk into the company TOC, a violin teacher thanked for pretending to believe practice claims. Jean wrote hers to her fourth-grade teacher and a GSB recommender.

ideas.idea: Turn bad outcomes into funny stories; a failed effort still yields material.
ideas.detail: Former student turned comedian Lucas Zelnick taught him this; his unanswered Sergey Brin emails became a running class bit, and Cherie jokes she hopes Brin never replies so the story continues.

ideas.idea: Good writing is learnable like jogging or piano, and better writing leads to better thinking and better opportunities.
ideas.detail: Half his class admits to writer's block; his goal is to make improving fun. A Tiger Sisters appearance got him a South by Southwest speaking gig, showing that the medium of visibility is changing.
